content: Pulmonary hypertension is a multifaceted condition that ultimately leads to right heart failure and premature death. Soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) stimulators represent a novel therapeutic class that has recently been approved for clinical use. This review aimed to assess the efficacy of sGC stimulators in treating pulmonary hypertension. The review included five randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving a total of 962 participants. These trials were relatively short in duration, lasting less than 16 weeks. Due to the diverse causes of pulmonary hypertension among participants, the results were analyzed according to specific subtypes of the condition. A pooled analysis demonstrated that sGC stimulators increased the six-minute walking distance (6MWD) by an average of 30.13 meters (95% confidence interval [CI]: 5.29 to 54.96 meters) across three studies involving 659 participants. However, subgroup analyses revealed differing effects based on the type of pulmonary hypertension. For pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), no significant improvement in 6MWD was observed (mean difference [MD]: 11.91 meters, 95% CI: −44.92 to 68.75 meters; 398 participants; 2 studies). In contrast, for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH), sGC stimulators improved 6MWD by 45 meters (95% CI: 23.87 to 66.13 meters; 261 participants; 1 study). Data for pulmonary hypertension associated with left heart disease were insufficient for pooled analysis. Notably, in PAH patients not receiving phosphodiesterase inhibitors, sGC stimulators increased 6MWD by 36 meters. Regarding mortality, pooled analysis showed no significant difference between sGC stimulators and placebo (Peto odds ratio [OR]: 0.57, 95% CI: 0.18 to 1.80). Secondary outcomes included an improvement in World Health Organization (WHO) functional class (OR: 1.53, 95% CI: 0.87 to 2.72; 858 participants; 4 studies), no significant effect on clinical worsening (OR: 0.45, 95% CI: 0.17 to 1.14; 842 participants; 3 studies), and a reduction in mean pulmonary artery pressure (MD: −2.77 mmHg, 95% CI: −4.96 to −0.58 mmHg; 744 participants; 5 studies). Serious adverse events did not differ significantly between treatment and placebo groups (OR: 1.12, 95% CI: 0.66 to 1.90; 818 participants; 5 studies). Subgroup analyses for PAH, left heart disease-associated pulmonary hypertension, and CTEPH also showed no significant differences in serious adverse events. It is critical to note that sGC stimulators should not be used in combination with phosphodiesterase-V inhibitors or nitrates due to the risk of severe hypotension. Additionally, the observed benefits in CTEPH are specific to patients with inoperable or recurrent disease. There is no evidence supporting the use of sGC stimulators in pulmonary hypertension associated with left heart disease or in pediatric populations. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE system. One outcome was rated as high quality, two as moderate quality, and eight as low or very low quality. This indicates that for many outcomes, the true effect may differ significantly from the estimates provided. The trials included in this review were generally well-conducted, with minor concerns regarding bias, and most employed an intention-to-treat analysis. In conclusion, sGC stimulators can reduce pulmonary artery pressures and improve exercise capacity in patients with PAH (who are treatment-naive or receiving a prostanoid or endothelin receptor antagonist) and in those with inoperable or recurrent CTEPH. These benefits are achieved without significant complications in these populations. However, their use is contraindicated in patients taking phosphodiesterase-V inhibitors or nitrates, and there is no evidence to support their use in left heart disease-associated pulmonary hypertension or in children. These findings are based on limited data, with some trial results unavailable for analysis.
